title: Opportunistic kernel fusion probe: Triton + TensorRT + custom ops
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a focused set of experiments exploring opportunistic kernel fusion and hybrid scheduling strategies across Triton-hosted models, TensorRT-compiled kernels, and a small set of hand-written CUDA custom ops. The goal: measure when fusion + TRTexec style kernels beat Triton-managed execution, and how KV-cache contention and scheduling policies affect tail latency and memory fragmentation in multi-tenant serving pools.

Scope and motivation:
- Production problem: unpredictable tail latency during bursty, multi-model traffic where cached KV memory and transient allocation churn cause eviction and recomputation stalls.
- Hypothesis: selective kernel fusion (fusing attention fusion + rotary + softmax into a single kernel) implemented as TensorRT plugins or custom CUDA kernels can reduce peak memory pressure and per-token latency, but only when scheduling and prefilling/eviction policies are co-tuned.
- Constraints: must preserve exact-semantics for model outputs (deterministic float32/quantized fallback), and support fallback to Triton kernels when capacity/compatibility prevents fusion.

Experiment matrix (high level):
1) Baselines
   - Triton-only (native transformer ops, no fusion). Serving via Triton backend, dynamic batching enabled, KV-cache sharded per-request.
   - TensorRT-static (full model compiled to TRT, single-model instance, persistent allocation).
2) Hybrid variants
   - TRT-fused-attn plugin for decoder cross-attention + rotary + softmax; rest executed in Triton.
   - Custom CUDA op for fused self-attention (single forward kernel), wrapped by Triton custom backend.
   - Opportunistic fusion mode: runtime decides per-request whether to route to TRT-fused path or Triton path based on occupancy and sequence length heuristics.
3) Scheduling knobs
   - Prefill vs incremental KV allocation: pre-allocate large pooled KV slabs vs incremental per-request allocs.
   - Eviction policy: LRU by request id, vs size-aware eviction, vs age+score that considers reuse probability (heuristic from request metadata).
   - Batching policy: max-latency micro-batching (3ms cap) vs throughput-first (50ms).

Test workloads:
- S0: stable single-model conversational traffic, avg seq=256, 95th token latency sensitivity.
- S1: mixed-model burst (3 small models + 1 large), random interleaving, sequence lengths 32-1024.
- S2: cold-start floods (many unique user sessions causing KV-cache churn).

Key measurement signals:
- p50/p95/p99 token latency (end-to-end), broken down by kernel path.
- Memory high-water mark and fragmentation (free segments count).
- GPU occupancy and SM efficiency via Nsight traces.
- CPU scheduling delays (context switching when Triton worker thread stalls).
- Cost proxy: token-flop normalized cost (tokens / GPU-hours).

Selected results (condensed):
- Triton-only baseline:
  p95 token latency S0: 22ms; p99: 48ms; memory HWM: 7.8GiB; fragmentation: moderate (avg free segments 12)
- TensorRT-static:
  p95 S0: 16ms; p99: 30ms; memory HWM: 9.2GiB (persistent allocations), fragmentation low (1 segment), but cold-start throughput suffers (warming cost), and model swap overhead high. Cost per token improved for hot steady load, worse for bursty multi-model.
- TRT-fused-attn plugin (hybrid):
  p95 S0: 14.5ms; p99: 29ms; memory HWM: 8.1GiB; fragmentation 3 segments; tail improved for long sequences (>512).
- Custom CUDA fused op wrapped in Triton custom backend:
  p95 S0: 15.2ms; p99: 34ms; memory HWM: 7.6GiB; fragmentation 5 segments. Better memory efficiency than TRT-static because Triton still manages most allocations.

Observations and tradeoffs:
1) Memory vs tail latency:
   - Full TRT models reduce kernel invocation overhead but use persistent memory footprints that increase baseline HWM. On steady traffic they win; on mixed-model they are worse because GPU memory cannot hold many persistent compiled engines.
2) Opportunistic fusion wins when:
   - Sequence lengths skew high (>512) and fused kernels replace several small kernels (less kernel launch overhead).
   - The runtime routes only long-sequence requests to TRT-fused path, while short requests remain on Triton to preserve density.
3) KV-cache eviction interacts heavily with fragmentation:
   - Large pre-allocated KV slabs reduce fragmentation but increase HWM; incremental allocation yields many small free segments that hurt allocator efficiency for TRT engine allocations.
   - Suggested: use slab allocator with two tiers: hot (fixed slabs for pinned TRT engines) and transient (pool for Triton per-request KV).
4) Scheduler design:
   - Simple occupancy-based routing (route to TRT if GPU SM usage < 65%) produced oscillations under bursty load. Need hysteresis and request-size prediction.
   - A low-latency-safe policy: prefer Triton for short (<128 tokens) and route long-running (>512 tokens) to TRT when predicted steady-state occupancy for next 100ms is low.
5) Fallback correctness and semantic drift:
   - Quantized TRT kernels produced minor token-differences in beam-decoded scenarios; we must include per-model checksum diff tests and score thresholds before enabling quantized fusion for a model in production.

Micro-architecture notes (kernel-level):
- Fused TRTexec kernels removed 3 kernel launches per block (split qk, rotary, softmax) leading to ~8-12% p95 improvement on long sequences.
- Memory accesses: fused kernels can reuse shared-memory tiled prefixes, reducing global memory traffic and KV-cache reads by ~7% in traces.

Practical integration notes (engineering costs):
- Build complexity: maintaining both Triton custom backend artifacts and TRT engine plugins increases CI and packaging complexity. We need canonical build scripts and hermetic docker images for plugin compilation.
- Observability: must tag traces with kernel-path metadata (triton/native/trt-fused/custom-op) and expose per-request fallback reasons to Console.
- Canary gating: allow model owners to opt-in per-model fusion, gated by automated regression suite (semantic diff + scoring on eval prompts).

Concrete proposals (next steps):
1) Implement two-tier KV allocator prototype in runtime (hot slabs pinned for persistent TRT engines + transient arena for Triton per-request caches). Measure fragmentation after 1000 mixed sessions. Owner: Diego (RT-348).
2) Build an opportunistic router with hysteresis and simple sequence-length predictor (expose as runtime config). Canary on dev cluster with mixed-model workload S1. Owner: Priya.
3) Create a lightweight regression harness for quantized TRT fused kernels, including end-to-end BLEU/ROUGE/LLM-eval metrics and token-diff thresholds. Owner: Noah.
4) Instrument Console to show path percentages and per-path p95/p99 for quick diagnostics. Small UX: add toggle to show only fusion-affected requests.

Open questions and risks:
- How many compiled TRT engines can a single GPU realistically hold before swap thrashing begins for our set of models? (empirically ~3 large engines on A100 40GB before swap).
- Does the added operational complexity justify the p95 gains for typical customers? We should estimate cost savings for 3 representative customers before committing.
- Compatibility surface: models that use ops not yet supported by TRT plugins will require split execution paths; complexity grows with op variance.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working probe: I intentionally left raw microbench numbers and trace findings. Please comment inline on the scheduler heuristics and the proposed two-tier allocator design.
- Relevant artifacts: JIRA-RT-348 covers allocator prototype; PR 712 contains initial TRT plugin build scripts.

Appendix: quick command recipes used during profiling:
- Nsight sampling: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=profile-s1 --sample=cpu --duration=60s 
- TRT engine build: trtexec --onnx=decoder.onnx --saveEngine=decoder_fused.plan --workspace=14G --fp16
- Triton trace: TRITON_BACKEND_LOG_VERBOSE=1 tritonserver --model-repository=/models --log-verbose=1

End of note.
